page: Vultr vx1-g-8c-32g is a general-purpose cloud server belonging to the VX1 Cloud Compute family. It features 8 dedicated vCPUs mapped to 4 physical cores with 2 threads per core, powered by an AMD EPYC processor running at 2.0 GHz on the x86_64 architecture. The CPU configuration includes 48 KB L1d cache, 1.0 MB L2 cache, and 32 MB L3 cache. It is equipped with 32.0 GB of system memory, providing 4.0 GB of RAM per core. Storage is provisioned via 1 GB of network-attached storage, and there are no onboard GPUs.

Benchmark results show a mix of top-tier single-core performance and average multi-core capabilities. The server achieves top-tier (top 10%) results in stress-ng single-core CPU performance, single-threaded gzip compression, single-threaded bzip3 decompression, and Geekbench text processing. However, multi-core metrics, including stress-ng multi-core CPU performance, multi-threaded bzip3 decompression, and Geekbench multi-core scores, fall into the average (middle 50%) category. Memory bandwidth tests for both small and large blocks, along with Passmark CPU and memory scores, also align with average tier performance.

The dedicated CPU allocation provides predictable performance per resource compared to shared-core alternatives, representing a stable hardware class for sustained workloads. This resource profile and performance distribution make the server appropriate for general-purpose workloads, software compilation, text processing, and moderate web serving, while showing limitations in highly parallelized multi-threaded tasks or larger language model inference.
description: Vultr vx1-g-8c-32g is a general-purpose cloud server from the VX1 Cloud Compute family, featuring 8 dedicated vCPUs on 4 physical AMD EPYC cores running at 2.0 GHz, paired with 32.0 GB of RAM and 1 GB of network storage. The server lacks a GPU. Performance benchmarks indicate a strong contrast between single-core and multi-core execution; single-core stress-ng, single-threaded gzip compression, and Geekbench text processing rank in the top 10%, while multi-core CPU performance, memory bandwidth, and database operations fall into the average tier. LLM inference shows strong text generation for small models but weak prompt processing for medium models. This configuration is appropriate for general-purpose applications, software compilation, and text processing tasks that benefit from dedicated CPU allocation and strong single-threaded performance, though it presents tradeoffs in highly parallelized or memory-intensive workloads.
